claim: C57BL/6J (B6) and CAST/EiJ (Cast) mouse strains exhibit one single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) difference every 120 bp on average.
source: Inbreeding caused random subsets of alleles segregating in their ancestral populations to become fixed, and as a consequence the two strains exhibit one single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) difference every 120 bp on average (Keane et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Keane et al., 2011

claim: 16 E11.5 F1 embryos were collected from reciprocal crosses between B6 and Cast.
source: We collected 16 E11.5 F1 embryos obtained from reciprocal crosses between B6 and Cast (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: The average SNP density in 3′ UTRs is approximately 1 SNP per 170 bp.
source: We profiled genome-wide gene expression using a 3′-biased RNA sequencing method, 3SEQ (Beck et al., 2010), in order to maximize SNP coverage in the 3′ UTRs, where the average SNP density is ∼1 SNP per 170 bp (compared to 1 SNP per 265 bp in the coding sequence).
evidence: Stated as a measurement in the manuscript

claim: The average SNP density in coding sequences is 1 SNP per 265 bp.
source: We profiled genome-wide gene expression using a 3′-biased RNA sequencing method, 3SEQ (Beck et al., 2010), in order to maximize SNP coverage in the 3′ UTRs, where the average SNP density is ∼1 SNP per 170 bp (compared to 1 SNP per 265 bp in the coding sequence).
evidence: Stated as a measurement in the manuscript

claim: The average fraction of reads supporting the B6 allele (B6 allele fraction, 'BAF') was 0.502.
source: Mapping of reads separately against the Cast (Keane et al., 2011) and B6 genomes allowed us to eliminate reference mapping bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as the average fraction of reads supporting the B6 allele (B6 allele fraction, 'BAF') was 0.502.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from sequencing data

claim: 1594 genes (23% of 6917 genes with sufficient reads covering SNPs) showed significant allele-specific expression (ASE).
source: Overall, out of a possible 6917 genes with sufficient reads covering SNPs, 1594 (23%) showed significant ASE (p < 0.01, paired t-test, Bonferroni corrected; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of sequencing data with specified significance threshold

claim: 154 N2 embryos were harvested at E11.5.
source: We next backcrossed F1 mice (derived from female B6 by male Cast crosses) with B6 parentals to obtain N2 embryos. We harvested 154 N2s at E11.5, performed 3SEQ, and quantified ASE in the approximately 50% of embryos that were heterozygous at each gene.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: There was excellent agreement between average BAF estimates from F1s and N2s with a correlation of rho = 0.77.
source: There was excellent agreement between average BAF estimates from F1s and N2s (Figure 2C; rho = 0.77).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of measurements

claim: Somites form every 90–120 minutes.
source: To quantify developmental progression for each embryo at the time of harvest, we counted the number of somites, which form every 90–120 min (Saga and Takeda, 2001) and ranged from 42 to 57 in our embryos.
evidence: Supported by citation to Saga and Takeda, 2001

claim: Somite numbers ranged from 42 to 57 in the embryos studied.
source: To quantify developmental progression for each embryo at the time of harvest, we counted the number of somites, which form every 90–120 min (Saga and Takeda, 2001) and ranged from 42 to 57 in our embryos.
evidence: Direct measurement from experimental samples

claim: 1796 genes showed significant correlation between total expression and somite number out of 7712 genes with moderate expression of at least 5 reads per million (RPM).
source: Of the 7712 genes with moderate expression of at least 5 reads per million (RPM), 1796 genes showed significant correlation between total expression and somite number (q < 0.05, Spearman correlation).
evidence: Statistical analysis of gene expression data

claim: Genes changing over the developmental time course were enriched for synaptogenesis (q = 2.2 × 10−8).
source: Genes changing over this developmental time course were enriched for a number of gene ontology (GO) categories indicative of important developmental processes occurring at E11.5, including synaptogenesis (q = 2.2 × 10−8, GOrilla) and eye lens formation (q = 5.8 × 10−7).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis with statistical significance

claim: Genes changing over the developmental time course were enriched for eye lens formation (q = 5.8 × 10−7).
source: Genes changing over this developmental time course were enriched for a number of gene ontology (GO) categories indicative of important developmental processes occurring at E11.5, including synaptogenesis (q = 2.2 × 10−8, GOrilla) and eye lens formation (q = 5.8 × 10−7).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis with statistical significance

claim: Genes changing over the developmental time course were enriched for blood microparticles (q = 9.6 × 10−7), which includes the globins.
source: A third significant GO category, blood microparticles (q = 9.6 × 10−7), includes the globins, which are beginning to undergo the transition from fetal to adult form over the developmental time period we assayed (Noordermeer and de Laat, 2008) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment analysis with statistical significance and citation

claim: Twelve genes show significant differential regulation between B6 and Cast alleles as a function of developmental timing.
source: By correlating ASE with somite number, we identified twelve genes that show significant differential regulation between B6 and Cast alleles as a function of developmental timing (q < 0.10, Spearman rho).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with specified significance threshold

claim: The B6 allele of the major adult beta globin (Hbb-b1) is delayed compared to the Cast allele (rho = 0.86, q < 10−14).
source: Both genes increase in absolute level and relative expression compared to fetal beta globins (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), but the B6 allele of the major form is delayed compared to the Cast allele (Figure 2E; rho = 0.86, q < 10−14), whereas the opposite occurs for the minor form (Figure 2F; rho = −0.51, q = 0.02).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of allele-specific expression over developmental time

claim: The Cast allele of the minor adult beta globin (Hbb-b2) is delayed compared to the B6 allele (rho = −0.51, q = 0.02).
source: Both genes increase in absolute level and relative expression compared to fetal beta globins (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), but the B6 allele of the major form is delayed compared to the Cast allele (Figure 2E; rho = 0.86, q < 10−14), whereas the opposite occurs for the minor form (Figure 2F; rho = −0.51, q = 0.02).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of allele-specific expression over developmental time

claim: By the end of the time course, the B6 and Cast alleles of both major and minor adult beta globins are equally expressed.
source: By the end of our time course, the alleles are equally expressed (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Observation from expression data shown in figures

claim: Transferrin increases in absolute expression but the Cast allele is delayed compared to the B6 allele (rho = −0.46, q = 0.02).
source: Transferrin also increases in absolute expression but the Cast allele is delayed compared to the B6 allele (rho = −0.46, q = 0.02; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of allele-specific expression

claim: Compensatory mechanisms have evolved in one or both strains to keep the overall regulatory dynamic of oxygen physiology stable during the fetal-to-adult hemoglobin switching period.
source: These results suggest that compensatory mechanisms have evolved in one or both strains to keep the overall regulatory dynamic of oxygen physiology stable during this important switching period.
evidence: Inference from the observed expression patterns of globin genes

claim: 31 genes with significant imprinting were found (p < 0.01, binomial test, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Consistent with previous studies in mouse embryos (Babak et al., 2008), we found a total of 31 genes with significant imprinting (Figure 2G–I; p < 0.01, binomial test, Bonferroni corrected), all of which had been previously identified.
evidence: Statistical analysis with specified significance threshold and comparison to previous studies

claim: All 31 imprinted genes identified had been previously identified.
source: Consistent with previous studies in mouse embryos (Babak et al., 2008), we found a total of 31 genes with significant imprinting (Figure 2G–I; p < 0.01, binomial test, Bonferroni corrected), all of which had been previously identified.
evidence: Comparison with existing literature

claim: Most imprinting generally acts uniformly across the embryo.
source: We note that the clear separation of most of the imprinted loci from the noise of the bulk of all expressed genes, with few exceptions (Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggests that most imprinting generally acts uniformly across the embryo, as expected from the methylation-based mechanism that sets the expression state of the regulated allele pre-zygotically (Reik et al., 1987).
evidence: Inference from data distribution pattern and supported by citation to methylation mechanism

claim: 331 embryonically expressed genes have total expression levels that differ significantly depending on the genetic background of the mother (Mann Whitney U test, p < 0.01, Bonferroni corrected).
source: To explore other genetically-encoded parental effects, we took advantage of the backcross design, in which N2 offspring have genotypically distinct parents. We identified a large number (n = 331) of embryonically expressed genes whose total expression levels differed significantly depending on the genetic background of the mother (Mann Whitney U test, p < 0.01, Bonferroni corrected), irrespective of the genotype of the embryo (Figure 3A,B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis with specified significance threshold

claim: Angptl4 expression increases 52% from an average of 107 RPM in embryos with an F1 mother to an average of 163 RPM in embryos with a B6 mother.
source: For example, Angptl4 expression increases 52% from an average of 107 RPM in embryos with an F1 mother to an average of 163 RPM in embryos with a B6 mother (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement of gene expression

claim: Maternal effect target genes exhibited up to a 3.5-fold difference in total expression level depending on genotype of the mother.
source: As for the magnitude of the effect, these maternal effect target genes exhibited up to a 3.5-fold (e.g., Polm: 2.5–11-fold at a 95% confidence interval) difference in total expression level depending on genotype of the mother.
evidence: Quantitative measurement with confidence interval

claim: All N2 embryos carry the B6 mitochondrial genome.
source: All F1s used for the backcross were derived from B6 female by Cast male matings, and therefore all N2 embryos carry the B6 mitochondrial genome, ruling out a confounding mitochondrial effect.
evidence: Logical inference from the breeding design

claim: The maternal effects were unchanged when considering sex, X chromosome genotype, litter, and developmental stage.
source: The maternal effects were unchanged when considering sex, X chromosome genotype, litter, and developmental stage.
evidence: Analysis controlling for potential confounding variables

claim: Maternal effect target genes were not imprinted or the result of contamination by maternally expressed transcripts.
source: Furthermore, for the vast majority of genes with SNP coverage, we were able to verify that maternal effect target genes were not imprinted or the result of contamination by maternally expressed transcripts.
evidence: Analysis to exclude alternative explanations

claim: Maternal genotype by itself was a better predictor of the maternal effects than maternal genotype in conjunction with embryonic genotype at any of the imprinted loci.
source: We found that maternal genotype by itself was a better predictor of the maternal effects than maternal genotype in conjunction with embryonic genotype at any of the imprinted loci, indicating that the maternal effects were not the result of trans effects downstream of imprinted genes.
evidence: Comparative statistical analysis

claim: Four genes were confirmed as maternal effect target genes using quantitative RT-PCR (qPCR).
source: To exclude the possibility of a batch effect in our 3SEQ data, we used quantitative RT-PCR (qPCR) to confirm 4 genes as maternal effect target genes.
evidence: Independent validation using orthogonal method

claim: Angptl4 functions in lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis, suggestive of a role in responding to the placental nutrient supply.
source: The most significant of the maternal effect target genes, Angptl4 (Figure 3C; p = 8 × 10−13 by 3SEQ, p = 1 × 10−11 by qPCR), functions in lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis, suggestive of a role in responding to the placental nutrient supply (Yoshida et al., 2002).
evidence: Known function from literature and inference about role

claim: Gpx3 is an antioxidant enzyme that acts in fat and glucose metabolism and has been associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes in mouse and human.
source: Similarly, Gpx3 (Figure 3B; p = 5 × 10−12 by 3SEQ, p = 6.6 × 10−4 by qPCR), a glutathione peroxidase, is an antioxidant enzyme that acts in fat and glucose metabolism and has been associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes in mouse and human (Lee et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2009).
evidence: Known function from literature citations

claim: Both Angptl4 and Gpx3 are transcriptionally regulated by the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor PPARγ.
source: Both of these genes are transcriptionally regulated by the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor PPARγ.
evidence: Statement of known regulatory relationship

claim: Genotyping and recombination analysis based on expressed SNPs divided the autosomes into 986 marker region blocks.
source: Genotyping and recombination analysis based on the expressed SNPs (Figure 4A) divided the autosomes into 986 marker region blocks, each separated by one or more recombination events that define candidate controlling loci.
evidence: Result of computational analysis of genotype data

claim: At a genome-wide significance level of q < 0.01, a total of 1034 eQTL were identified.
source: At a genome-wide significance level of q < 0.01, we identified a total of 1034 eQTL.
evidence: Statistical analysis with specified significance threshold

claim: 1017 of the 1034 eQTL (98%) mapped close to the target gene, suggesting cis-regulation as the underlying mechanism.
source: 1017 of these eQTL (98%) mapped close to the target gene (Figure 4B), suggesting cis-regulation as the underlying mechanism.
evidence: Analysis of eQTL genomic locations and inference about mechanism

claim: A gene's difference in expression between heterozygotes and homozygotes could accurately predict its allelic ratio as assayed by ASE (rho = 0.58, n = 4821).
source: A gene's difference in expression between heterozygotes and homozygotes could accurately predict its allelic ratio as assayed by ASE (Figure 4C). This high correlation (rho = 0.58, n = 4821; rho = 0.70 when considering only the n = 1000 genes with the highest allele-specific read coverage) provides a systematic validation of the large effect of embryonic cis-regulatory polymorphisms on expression phenotype.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between two measurements

claim: When considering only the n = 1000 genes with the highest allele-specific read coverage, the correlation between predicted and measured allelic ratio is rho = 0.70.
source: This high correlation (rho = 0.58, n = 4821; rho = 0.70 when considering only the n = 1000 genes with the highest allele-specific read coverage) provides a systematic validation of the large effect of embryonic cis-regulatory polymorphisms on expression phenotype.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis on subset of data

claim: Few trans-eQTL were found regardless of FDR cutoff.
source: In contrast to the large number of cis-eQTL, we found few trans-eQTL regardless of FDR cutoff (Figure 5A).
evidence: Result of eQTL analysis across multiple significance thresholds

claim: After the top 3 trans-eQTL, significance drops off rapidly compared to background, unlike for the cis-eQTL.
source: After the top 3 (each comprising a controlling locus–target gene pair, e.g., Figure 5B), significance drops off rapidly compared to background, unlike for the cis-eQTL (Figure 5C).
evidence: Observation from statistical analysis shown in figure

claim: Neither strong cis-eQTL nor ASE loci are enriched for trans-eQTL.
source: However, we found that neither strong cis-eQTL nor ASE loci are enriched for trans-eQTL.
evidence: Result of enrichment analysis

claim: Application of a random forest model that simultaneously considers developmental progression (number of somites) and genotype did not enrich for trans-eQTL.
source: Finally, application of a random forest model (Michaelson et al., 2010; Francesconi and Lehner, 2014) that simultaneously considers developmental progression (number of somites) and genotype also did not enrich for trans-eQTL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Result of alternative statistical modeling approach

claim: The number of comparable trans-eQTL is about 1% that of cis-eQTL.
source: We estimate that the number of comparable trans-eQTL is about 1% that of cis-eQTL.
evidence: Quantitative estimate from data analysis

claim: Permutation tests revealed a significant signal (p < 10−24 KS test) in support of trans-eQTL hotspots.
source: Permutation tests revealed a significant signal (p < 10−24 KS test, Figure 5D) in support of hotspots, but no specific candidates.
evidence: Statistical permutation test

claim: Strong ASE genes were not substantially more likely to act as hotspots than weaker ASE genes (p = 0.20, KS test).
source: Reinforcing the above result that ASE genes do not act as trans-controlling loci, strong ASE genes were not substantially more likely to act as hotspots than weaker ASE genes (Figure 5D; p = 0.20, KS test).
evidence: Statistical comparison test

claim: At E11.5 stage of embryogenesis, there is no evidence for downstream propagation of genetically controlled expression level differences.
source: Therefore, at this stage of embryogenesis, we found no evidence for downstream propagation of genetically controlled expression level differences.
evidence: Conclusion from multiple lines of analysis

claim: All previously published eQTL studies conducted in adult tissues showed a substantially higher proportion of trans-eQTL than embryos.
source: After sampling individuals to match the same number of total eQTL found at an FDR of 0.05, we found that all previously published studies conducted in adult tissues showed a substantially higher proportion of trans-eQTL than did our embryos (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Comparative analysis with published datasets

claim: The result that embryos have fewer trans-eQTL than adult tissues was robust to varying the sample size from the previously published data, to whether p-values or FDR was used to assess significance, and to varying the thresholds for comparing proportions of trans-eQTL across the ranked eQTL.
source: This result was robust to varying the sample size from the previously published data, to whether p-values or FDR was used to assess significance, and to varying the thresholds for comparing proportions of trans-eQTL across the ranked eQTL.
evidence: Sensitivity analysis of comparative results

claim: Embryonic trans-eQTL are subject to elevated selective constraint compared to adult tissues.
source: Based on this result and our high power to detect cis-eQTL even at low FDR, we conclude that embryonic trans-eQTL are subject to elevated selective constraint compared to adult tissues.
evidence: Conclusion from comparative analysis and power considerations

claim: ASE genes were significantly depleted of GO categories related to organ development (p = 6 × 10−5, q = 0.05).
source: In support of this hypothesis, ASE genes were significantly depleted of GO categories related to organ development (p = 6 × 10−5, q = 0.05), as well as gene regulation (p = 1 × 10−4, q = 0.07), and transcription factors (p = 3 × 10−5, q = 0.03), demonstrating constraints on variation in core regulatory genes.
evidence: Gene ontology depletion analysis with statistical significance

claim: ASE genes were significantly depleted of GO categories related to gene regulation (p = 1 × 10−4, q = 0.07).
source: In support of this hypothesis, ASE genes were significantly depleted of GO categories related to organ development (p = 6 × 10−5, q = 0.05), as well as gene regulation (p = 1 × 10−4, q = 0.07), and transcription factors (p = 3 × 10−5, q = 0.03), demonstrating constraints on variation in core regulatory genes.
evidence: Gene ontology depletion analysis with statistical significance

claim: ASE genes were significantly depleted of GO categories related to transcription factors (p = 3 × 10−5, q = 0.03).
source: In support of this hypothesis, ASE genes were significantly depleted of GO categories related to organ development (p = 6 × 10−5, q = 0.05), as well as gene regulation (p = 1 × 10−4, q = 0.07), and transcription factors (p = 3 × 10−5, q = 0.03), demonstrating constraints on variation in core regulatory genes.
evidence: Gene ontology depletion analysis with statistical significance

claim: Evolutionary constraint at the DNA sequence level was lowest in the most significant cis-eQTL (rho = −0.14, p = 6 × 10−13; n = 2788).
source: Furthermore, we found that evolutionary constraint at the DNA sequence level (Cooper et al., 2005; Davydov et al., 2010) was lowest in the most significant cis-eQTL (Figure 5G; rho = −0.14, p = 6 × 10−13; n = 2788).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between conservation scores and eQTL significance

claim: ASE magnitude of effect correlated negatively with evolutionary constraint (rho = −0.10, p = 9 × 10−8, n = 2612).
source: Similarly, ASE magnitude of effect correlated negatively with evolutionary constraint (rho = −0.10, p = 9 × 10−8, n = 2612), whereas cis-eQTL in adult mouse tissues showed no correlation (|rho| < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis

claim: cis-eQTL in adult mouse tissues showed no correlation with evolutionary constraint (|rho| < 0.05).
source: Similarly, ASE magnitude of effect correlated negatively with evolutionary constraint (rho = −0.10, p = 9 × 10−8, n = 2612), whereas cis-eQTL in adult mouse tissues showed no correlation (|rho| < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis on published data

claim: The strong enrichment for cis-eQTL/ASE in less conserved genes is unique to embryos.
source: Thus, the strong enrichment for cis-eQTL/ASE in less conserved genes is unique to embryos.
evidence: Conclusion from comparative analysis between embryonic and adult data

claim: The two mouse strains exhibit SNPs at 17.7 million sites, about sixfold more than the heterozygosity in African humans.
source: Our two mouse strains exhibit SNPs at 17.7 million sites, about sixfold more than the heterozygosity in African humans (1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2012).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with human data from cited source

claim: Missense polymorphisms are severely underrepresented genome-wide and exhibit lower derived allele frequencies relative to other genomic sites, reflecting the global predominance of purifying selection.
source: Missense polymorphisms are severely underrepresented genome-wide and exhibit lower derived allele frequencies relative to other genomic sites (1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2012), reflecting the global predominance of purifying selection.
evidence: Known pattern from literature and interpretation

claim: The signal of purifying selection is weaker but still substantial for noncoding gene regulatory sites.
source: This signal of purifying selection is weaker but still substantial for noncoding gene regulatory sites (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2007).
evidence: Known pattern from literature

claim: Substantial neutral divergence of molecular phenotype (gene expression) can accumulate in the form of cis-regulatory variation even under strong evolutionary constraint at the organismal (embryonic) level.
source: These findings support the idea of the developmental hourglass model (Domazet-Lošo and Tautz, 2010; Kalinka et al., 2010) while suggesting that substantial neutral divergence of molecular phenotype (gene expression) can accumulate in the form of cis-regulatory variation even under strong evolutionary constraint at the organismal (embryonic) level.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of evolutionary theory

claim: Incorporating developmental timing (somite number) into the eQTL model did not alter the balance between cis- and trans-regulation.
source: Perhaps because of the nearness of our embryos to the mouse phylotypic stage, or because of fundamental differences between mice and worms, we found that incorporating developmental timing (i.e., somite number) into our eQTL model did not alter the balance between cis- and trans-regulation.
evidence: Result of statistical modeling with developmental stage as covariate

claim: Somite number was correlated with significant changes in ASE, indicating differential developmental timing of gene expression between the Cast and B6 strains.
source: Somite number was, however, correlated with significant changes in ASE, indicating differential developmental timing of gene expression between the Cast and B6 strains.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis and interpretation

claim: Alleles of several hemoglobin-related genes, including the adult beta globins and transferrin, were expressed at differing levels between the strains at early stages of the fetal-to-adult hemoglobin transition, but then equalize by the end of the developmental time course.
source: In particular, we found that alleles of several hemoglobin-related genes, including the adult beta globins and transferrin, were expressed at differing levels between the strains at early stages of the fetal-to-adult hemoglobin transition, but then equalize by the end of our developmental time course.
evidence: Observation from time-course expression data

claim: The good agreement between eQTL and ASE suggests that the majority of local eQTL are indeed cis-eQTL.
source: However, the good agreement between eQTL and ASE suggests that the majority of our local eQTL are indeed cis-eQTL.
evidence: Inference from correlation between two independent measurements

claim: Nearly all imprinted genes showed very strong allelic bias, meaning that the epigenetically silenced allele is expressed at only low levels across the embryo.
source: Because of the large number of embryos collected and individually sequenced for our study, we were able to accurately quantify ASE mean and standard deviation for thousands of genes. When stratifying embryos by side of cross, we found that nearly all imprinted genes showed very strong allelic bias, meaning that the epigenetically silenced allele is expressed at only low levels across the embryo.
evidence: Observation from allele-specific expression measurements

claim: The genotype of the mother plays an important role in regulating gene expression during embryogenesis, affecting the expression of hundreds of genes.
source: Our results demonstrate that the genotype of the mother plays an important role in regulating gene expression, not just after birth, as has been previously suggested, but also during embryogenesis, affecting the expression of hundreds of genes (Bult and Lynch, 1997; Weaver et al., 2004; Wolf et al., 2011).
evidence: Conclusion from maternal effect analysis

claim: What is usually thought of as familial environment may have a substantial heritable genetic component exerting an effect not on the generation carrying it but on the offspring.
source: The implications of this finding are significant for human genetic twin, familial, and genome-wide association studies. What is usually thought of as familial environment [e.g., Grundberg et al. (2012)] may have a substantial heritable genetic component exerting an effect not on the generation carrying it but on the offspring.
evidence: Inference about implications of maternal effects findings

claim: The maternal effect is more likely acting through the placenta's role of transmitting nutrients, hormones or other factors to the embryo.
source: While we cannot rule out an epigenetic or RNA-mediated mechanism underlying this regulation, it is more likely acting through the placenta's role of transmitting nutrients, hormones or other factors to the embryo.
evidence: Inference about mechanism based on gene functions

claim: Maternal effect target genes may be at least partly responsible for the previously observed effect of maternal genotype on pre-natal growth.
source: We hypothesize that these maternal effect target genes continue to be expressed differently depending on maternal genotype, and may be at least partly responsible for the previously observed effect of maternal genotype on pre-natal growth (Cowley et al., 1989; Wolf et al., 2011).
evidence: Hypothesis connecting current findings to previous observations

claim: cis-regulatory variation caused the largest divergence in overall gene expression in mouse embryos, affecting over 1000 genes with up to sevenfold differences in expression levels between the strains.
source: In summary, using our hybrid ASE/eQTL approach we were able to assay all four types of genetic variation in gene expression regulation. We found that cis-regulatory variation caused the largest divergence in overall gene expression in mouse embryos, affecting over 1000 genes with up to sevenfold differences in expression levels between the strains.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple analyses

claim: Only approximately 10 trans-eQTL were identified genomewide.
source: These cis-regulatory variants did not translate into trans-regulatory divergence, and we identified only ∼10 trans-eQTL genomewide.
evidence: Result of eQTL analysis

claim: Imprinting affected the allelic balance of dozens of genes, generally resulting in complete or nearly complete silencing of the inactive allele.
source: Imprinting affected the allelic balance of dozens of genes, generally resulting in complete or nearly complete silencing of the inactive allele.
evidence: Summary of imprinting analysis results

claim: The number of maternal effect targets is approximately 1/3 as many genes as cis-regulatory effects, with maximal effect size of up to 3.5-fold difference or approximately 1/2 as large.
source: The number of maternal effect targets, and their overall significance, are only slightly more modest than cis-regulatory effects, but nonetheless substantial, with approximately 1/3 as many genes involved, and maximal effect size of up to 3.5-fold difference or approximately 1/2 as large.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of effect sizes

claim: Maternal effects can play a substantial genetic role in determining embryonic gene expression patterns.
source: Given this context, it is clear that maternal effects can play a substantial genetic role in determining embryonic gene expression patterns.
evidence: Conclusion from magnitude of maternal effects observed

claim: Maternal effects contribute to evolutionary divergence, allowing expression heterogeneity in the embryo to build as a result of differences in the adult mother, where gene regulatory networks show less evolutionary constraint than in the developing embryo.
source: We speculate that maternal effects contribute to evolutionary divergence, allowing expression heterogeneity in the embryo to build as a result of differences in the adult mother, where gene regulatory networks show less evolutionary constraint than in the developing embryo.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about evolutionary implications

claim: E11.5 is equivalent to roughly 40 days of gestation in human.
source: We focus on embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5), which is equivalent to roughly 40 days of gestation in human.
evidence: Statement of developmental stage equivalence

claim: E11.5 is a time characterized by organogenesis, rapid growth of the brain and limbs, increasingly complex and localized pattern formation, and consequently substantial constraints on allowable phenotypic variation.
source: It is a time characterized by organogenesis, rapid growth of the brain and limbs, increasingly complex and localized pattern formation, and consequently substantial constraints on allowable phenotypic variation.
evidence: Description of developmental stage based on established knowledge

claim: Fewer than 200 genes are imprinted in mice and humans.
source: A recent genome-wide survey estimated that fewer than 200 genes are imprinted in mice and humans (Babak et al., 2008).
evidence: Estimate from cited literature

claim: Imprinting is thought to play a critical role in early embryonic and placental development in mammals and has been shown to influence post-natal health and behavior.
source: Imprinting is thought to play a critical role in early embryonic and placental development in mammals and has been shown to influence post-natal health and behavior [Reviewed in Peters (2014)].
evidence: Summary of known roles from review article

claim: Maternal effects have been shown to be important during embryonic development, leading to differences in the birth weight of mice depending on the genotype of the mother.
source: Maternal effects have been shown to be important during embryonic development, leading to differences in the birth weight of mice depending on the genotype of the mother (Cowley et al., 1989; Wolf et al., 2011).
evidence: Known findings from cited literature

claim: Neither the causal molecular mechanism for maternal effects in the mother nor the responding genes in the embryo have been identified.
source: However, neither the causal molecular mechanism for these effects in the mother nor the responding genes in the embryo have been identified and few studies to date have discriminated between prenatal and postnatal effects.
evidence: Statement about gaps in existing knowledge

claim: Maternal effects likely contribute to the heritability of complex traits but have been confounded with family structure in mouse as well as human studies.
source: Maternal effects likely contribute to the heritability of complex traits but have been confounded with family structure in mouse as well as human studies (Mott et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about methodological challenges from cited literature

claim: In adult flies and mice, cis and trans regulatory variants frequently target the same genes, often with opposite, compensatory effects on the target's expression.
source: In adult flies and mice, these analyses have demonstrated that cis and trans regulatory variants frequently target the same genes, often with opposite, compensatory effects on the target's expression (McManus et al., 2010; Goncalves et al., 2012).
evidence: Known pattern from cited literature

claim: High-throughput sequencing methods can directly identify genes with cis-regulatory variants through genome-wide studies of ASE patterns.
source: Recent genome-wide studies of ASE patterns across many individuals have demonstrated the ability of high-throughput sequencing methods to directly identify genes with cis-regulatory variants (Montgomery et al., 2010; Pickrell et al., 2010).
evidence: Known capability from cited literature

claim: The strongest genetic variation in expression regulation generally occurs in variants located proximally to their target genes, presumably acting in cis.
source: Genome-wide eQTL studies have demonstrated that the strongest genetic variation in expression regulation generally occurs in variants located proximally to their target genes, presumably acting in cis.
evidence: Known pattern from eQTL studies

claim: trans-regulatory variants affect both alleles of each target gene and can affect expression of many genes simultaneously, resulting in a large aggregate effect.
source: While typically fewer in number, trans-regulatory variants affect both alleles of each target gene and can affect expression of many genes simultaneously, resulting in a large aggregate effect.
evidence: Known characteristics of trans-regulation

claim: eQTL studies have demonstrated dynamic trans-regulatory variation during Caenorhabditis elegans larval development.
source: First, eQTL studies have demonstrated dynamic trans-regulatory variation during Caenorhabditis elegans larval development (Francesconi and Lehner, 2014).
evidence: Known finding from cited literature
